title: Performance analysis and bottleneck hunting
summary: Find the real bottleneck behind 'the machine is slow' by measuring CPU, memory, disk, and the often-missed resources. Capture and read an Event Tracing for Windows profile with WPR and WPA.
objectives: Decompose 'slow' into a measurable bottleneck across CPU, memory, disk, and GPU
Use Performance Monitor counters to distinguish saturation from latency
Identify hard page faults and committed-memory pressure versus working-set churn
Capture a CPU and disk profile with Windows Performance Recorder (WPR)
Open and read the trace in Windows Performance Analyzer (WPA) to find the hot stack
Tell a genuine resource bottleneck apart from a scheduling or contention problem

quiz.q: A machine feels slow but CPU sits at 30%, RAM at 50%, and disk queue is low. Which resource is the most likely culprit you have NOT yet measured?
options: Disk latency / per-IO response time, or GPU and network waits
quiz.why: Low utilisation with poor responsiveness points to latency, not saturation — a disk that is idle but answering each IO slowly, or waits on GPU/network. Utilisation percentages alone never reveal latency.

quiz.q: Which PerfMon counter best indicates memory pressure forcing the system to hit disk?
options: Memory\Pages/sec combined with hard faults (page reads/sec)
quiz.why: Hard page faults — pages read from disk because they were paged out — are the real cost. Pages/sec alongside hard fault rate reveals the system thrashing; Available MBytes alone can look fine while paging hurts.

quiz.q: What does Windows Performance Recorder (WPR) actually capture?
options: A static snapshot of running processes
Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) events including sampled CPU stacks and disk IO
quiz.why: WPR drives ETW providers to record a time-based trace — sampled CPU call stacks, context switches, disk and file IO, and more — which WPA then analyses. It is a trace, not a snapshot or a dump.

quiz.q: In WPA, you see a thread spending most of its time in 'Ready' but not 'Running'. What does that indicate?
options: The thread is CPU-bound and saturating a core
The thread is runnable but waiting for a CPU — a scheduling/contention problem, not raw CPU shortage
quiz.why: Time in Ready means the thread could run but no core was available to it — a contention or priority issue. That is a different fix from a thread genuinely burning CPU in Running state.

quiz.q: Name one reason high CPU utilisation can still mean the CPU is NOT the bottleneck.
quiz.answer: The CPU may be busy spinning on a lock, handling interrupts/DPCs from a misbehaving driver, or busy-waiting on slow IO — so it looks saturated while the real constraint is contention or a downstream device, not compute capacity.
quiz.why: Utilisation measures busyness, not useful work; high CPU from lock contention, interrupt storms, or busy-waiting is a symptom of a different root cause.

quiz.q: Why capture a timed WPR trace instead of just reading Task Manager?
quiz.answer: Task Manager shows instantaneous, aggregated utilisation; a WPR/ETW trace records the actual call stacks, context switches, and IO over time, so you can see which module and which stack is consuming the resource and whether the cost is CPU, wait, or IO.
quiz.why: Root cause needs the responsible stack and the wait analysis over time, which only a trace provides — Task Manager tells you something is busy, not what or why.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Performance Monitor and counters

body_markdown:
## 'Slow' is not a measurement

The word **slow** is a symptom, never a cause. Your first job is to turn it into a number: which resource is constrained, and is the problem **saturation** (the resource is maxed out) or **latency** (the resource is idle but answering slowly)? These have opposite fixes, and utilisation percentages alone cannot tell them apart. A disk at 5% busy that takes 40 ms per IO will make a machine feel terrible while every dashboard looks green.

## The four-resource sweep, plus the ones people miss

Start with the obvious four — **CPU, memory, disk, network** — but go beyond utilisation. For each, ask both *how busy* and *how slow per operation*.

```text
CPU     : % usage, but also queue length and DPC/interrupt time
Memory  : Available MB, AND hard page-fault rate (paging to disk)
Disk    : % busy, AND avg sec/transfer (latency per IO)
Network : throughput, AND round-trip latency and retransmits
```

Then check the ones people forget: **GPU** (compositor and rendering waits), **handle/thread leaks**, and **lock contention**. A process climbing in handles or threads over hours is a leak you will only see by trending.

## Counters that reveal the truth

Performance Monitor exposes the diagnostic counters Task Manager hides.

```powershell
# Sample the high-value counters once a second for 30 seconds
Get-Counter -Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time',
  '\Memory\Available MBytes',
  '\Memory\Pages/sec',
  '\PhysicalDisk(_Total)\Avg. Disk sec/Transfer',
  '\System\Processor Queue Length' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 30
```

Memory pressure shows up as **hard page faults** (`Pages/sec` driven by reads from disk), not as low Available MB alone. A persistently non-zero `Processor Queue Length` means threads are waiting for a core — contention, not raw CPU shortage.

## Capturing a real profile with WPR

Utilisation tells you *something* is busy; a trace tells you *what* and *why*. **Windows Performance Recorder (WPR)** drives **Event Tracing for Windows (ETW)** to capture sampled CPU stacks, context switches, and disk IO over time.

```powershell
# Start a CPU + disk profile, reproduce the slowness, then stop
wpr -start CPU -start DiskIO
# ... reproduce the slow operation now ...
wpr -stop C:\evidence\slow.etl
```

## Reading it in WPA

Open the `.etl` in **Windows Performance Analyzer (WPA)**. In the CPU Usage (Sampled) graph, expand by process then by stack to find the **hot stack** — the call path consuming the most samples. Crucially, read the thread states: time in **Running** is real CPU work; time in **Ready** means the thread was runnable but starved of a core (contention); time in **Waiting** points at IO or a lock. A thread mostly in Ready is a scheduling problem, not a CPU-capacity problem — a completely different fix.

## Your task

Reproduce a slow scenario on a test machine (or run a CPU/IO-heavy workload). Capture 30 seconds of the PerfMon counters above with `Get-Counter` and decide whether you are seeing saturation or latency. Then capture a WPR trace covering the slow operation, open it in WPA, and identify the hot stack and the dominant thread state (Running, Ready, or Waiting). Write a two-paragraph finding: name the constrained resource, classify it as saturation vs latency vs contention, and state the responsible module from the stack.

slides.title: Performance analysis and bottleneck hunting
slides.sub: Month 1 - Advanced Troubleshooting & Root Cause Analysis  |  Lesson 3
slides.narration: Slow is the vaguest ticket you'll ever get. In this lesson we turn slow into a number. You'll learn to separate saturation from latency, to read the performance counters Task Manager hides, and to capture a real trace with the Windows Performance Recorder so you can point at the exact stack that's eating the machine.

slides.title: 'Slow' is a symptom, not a cause
bullets: Turn 'slow' into a measured, constrained resource.
Saturation: the resource is maxed out.
Latency: the resource is idle but answers slowly.
These have opposite fixes — utilisation can't tell them apart.
slides.narration: First principle: slow is a symptom, never a cause. Your job is to turn it into a number — which resource is constrained, and is it saturation or latency? Saturation means the resource is maxed out. Latency means it's idle but answering slowly. These have completely opposite fixes. A disk that's only five percent busy but takes forty milliseconds per I O will make a machine feel awful while every dashboard looks green.

slides.title: Measure busy AND slow per operation
bullets: CPU: usage, plus queue length and DPC time.
Memory: available MB, plus hard page-fault rate.
Disk: percent busy, plus seconds per transfer.
Network: throughput, plus round-trip latency.
slides.code:
CPU     : % usage + queue length + DPC time
Memory  : Available MB + hard page faults
Disk    : % busy + avg sec/transfer
Network : throughput + RTT + retransmits
slides.narration: For each resource, ask two questions, not one: how busy is it, and how slow is each operation? For C P U, look at usage but also queue length and time spent in deferred procedure calls. For memory, available megabytes but also the hard page-fault rate. For disk, percent busy but also average seconds per transfer. For network, throughput but also round-trip latency. The second number is the one people skip, and it's usually where the answer is.

slides.title: The resources people forget
bullets: GPU: compositor and rendering waits.
Handle and thread leaks — only visible by trending.
Lock contention — high CPU doing no useful work.
A process climbing in handles over hours is a leak.
slides.narration: Beyond the famous four, check the ones people forget. The G P U can stall the desktop compositor. Handle and thread leaks only reveal themselves when you trend a process over hours. And lock contention can pin a core at a hundred percent while doing no useful work at all. If a process is steadily climbing in handles across an afternoon, that's a leak, and you'll only catch it by watching the trend, not a single snapshot.

slides.title: Counters that reveal the truth
bullets: PerfMon exposes what Task Manager hides.
Hard page faults reveal memory thrashing, not Available MB.
Processor Queue Length reveals core contention.
Sample over time, not a single instant.
slides.code:
Get-Counter -Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time',
  '\Memory\Available MBytes',
  '\Memory\Pages/sec',
  '\PhysicalDisk(_Total)\Avg. Disk sec/Transfer',
  '\System\Processor Queue Length' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 30
slides.narration: Performance Monitor exposes the diagnostic counters Task Manager hides. Use Get-Counter to sample them once a second. Memory pressure shows up as hard page faults — pages read back from disk — not as low available megabytes alone. And a processor queue length that stays above zero means threads are waiting for a core. That's contention, not a raw C P U shortage. Always sample over time, never trust a single instant.

slides.title: Capture a profile with WPR
bullets: Utilisation says something is busy; a trace says what and why.
WPR drives Event Tracing for Windows.
It records sampled CPU stacks, context switches, disk IO.
Start, reproduce the slowness, then stop to a .etl file.
slides.code:
wpr -start CPU -start DiskIO
# ... reproduce the slow operation ...
wpr -stop C:\evidence\slow.etl
slides.narration: Utilisation tells you something is busy. A trace tells you what and why. The Windows Performance Recorder, w-p-r, drives Event Tracing for Windows to capture sampled C P U call stacks, context switches, and disk I O over time. The workflow is simple: w p r dash start C P U, dash start disk I O, reproduce the slow operation, then w p r dash stop to an e-t-l file. That e t l is your evidence.

slides.title: Read the trace in WPA
bullets: Open the .etl in Windows Performance Analyzer.
Expand CPU Usage Sampled by process, then by stack.
Find the hot stack — the path with the most samples.
Read thread states to know what kind of problem it is.
slides.narration: Open that e t l in the Windows Performance Analyzer, w-p-a. In the C P U Usage Sampled graph, expand by process and then by stack to find the hot stack — the call path consuming the most samples. That single view often names the culprit module directly. But don't stop at the stack; read the thread states next, because they tell you what kind of problem you actually have.

slides.title: Running vs Ready vs Waiting
bullets: Running: real CPU work being done.
Ready: runnable but starved of a core — contention.
Waiting: blocked on IO or a lock.
A thread mostly in Ready is a scheduling problem.
slides.narration: In W P A, the thread state breakdown is gold. Time in Running is genuine C P U work. Time in Ready means the thread could run but no core was free for it — that's contention or a priority problem. Time in Waiting means it's blocked on I O or a lock. So a thread that's mostly Ready is a scheduling problem, not a C P U-capacity problem, and that's a completely different fix. This is how you avoid throwing more cores at a contention bug.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Separate saturation from latency from contention.
Use Get-Counter for hard faults and queue length.
Capture with WPR, analyse the hot stack in WPA.
Task: profile a slow scenario and name the constraint.
